# Crystal Lattices {#sec-crystal-lattices}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pedagogical Context [NOT DERIVED FROM FTD]
This chapter provides **standard crystallography context**. While FTD proposes a mechanism for crystal structure (see callout below), **no quantitative predictions** (lattice constants, crystal energies) are derived from FTD axioms at this scale. The mechanisms described are [CONJECTURE].
:::

*"Order in the solid state"*

::: {.callout-note}
## Key Revelation
Crystals are not random: they follow strict geometric rules. Only 14 fundamental lattice types exist in 3D, and all crystalline matter fits into these patterns.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## How FTD Proposes Crystal Structure [CONJECTURE]
The 14 Bravais lattices are *proposed* to emerge from FTD's discrete substrate:

- **The simulation lattice is cubic**, providing the natural coordinate system
- **Atomic positions** are minima of the flux potential
- **Lattice constants** emerge from equilibrium between attractive (strong/EM) and repulsive (Pauli) flux gradients
- **Crystal symmetries** reflect the point group symmetries of the flux field

The discrete nature of FTD space naturally admits discrete crystal structures.
:::

## Bravais Lattices

There are exactly 14 ways to fill 3D space with a repeating pattern.

### The Seven Crystal Systems

| System | Lattices | Angles | Lengths | Example |
|--------|----------|--------|---------|---------|
| Cubic | 3 | 90°, 90°, 90° | a = b = c | NaCl, Fe, Cu |
| Tetragonal | 2 | 90°, 90°, 90° | a = b $\neq$ c | Tin, $\text{TiO}_2$ |
| Orthorhombic | 4 | 90°, 90°, 90° | a $\neq$ b $\neq$ c | Sulfur |
| Hexagonal | 1 | 90°, 90°, 120° | a = b $\neq$ c | Graphite, Zn |
| Trigonal | 1 | $\alpha = \beta = \gamma \neq 90°$ | a = b = c | Quartz |
| Monoclinic | 2 | 90°, $\beta$, 90° | a $\neq$ b $\neq$ c | Gypsum |
| Triclinic | 1 | $\alpha \neq \beta \neq \gamma$ | a $\neq$ b $\neq$ c | Most organics |

## Cubic Lattices

The most common metallic structures.

### Simple Cubic (SC)

![Simple cubic lattice: atoms at corners only, coordination number 6, packing efficiency 52%.](../../media/images/fig-simple-cubic.png){#fig-simple-cubic}

- **Coordination**: 6 nearest neighbors
- **Packing efficiency**: 52%
- **Example**: Polonium

### Body-Centered Cubic (BCC)

![Body-centered cubic lattice: atoms at corners plus one atom in the center of the cube.](../../media/images/fig-bcc.png){#fig-bcc}

- **Coordination**: 8 nearest neighbors
- **Packing efficiency**: 68%
- **Examples**: Fe, W, Cr, Na

### Face-Centered Cubic (FCC)

![Face-centered cubic lattice: atoms at corners plus atoms at the center of each face.](../../media/images/fig-fcc.png){#fig-fcc}

- **Coordination**: 12 nearest neighbors
- **Packing efficiency**: 74%
- **Examples**: Cu, Al, Au, Ag

## Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP)

Alternative to FCC with same packing efficiency.

![Hexagonal close-packed lattice: alternating layers in ABABAB stacking pattern.](../../media/images/fig-hcp.png){#fig-hcp}

- **Stacking sequence**: ABABAB... (2 layers repeat)
- **Coordination**: 12 nearest neighbors
- **Packing efficiency**: 74%
- **Examples**: Mg, Zn, Ti

### FCC vs HCP

Both are close-packed (74%) but different stacking:
- FCC: ABCABC... (3 layers repeat)
- HCP: ABABAB... (2 layers repeat)

## Diamond Cubic

![Diamond cubic lattice: each atom tetrahedrally bonded to four neighbors.](../../media/images/fig-diamond-cubic.png){#fig-diamond-cubic}

Each atom bonds to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement, creating an open structure with remarkable properties:

- **Coordination**: 4 nearest neighbors
- **Packing efficiency**: 34% (very open structure)
- **Examples**: C (diamond), Si, Ge

## Defects

Real crystals have imperfections.

### Point Defects

| Type | Description | Effect |
|------|-------------|--------|
| Vacancy | Missing atom | Diffusion |
| Interstitial | Extra atom | Strengthening |
| Substitutional | Wrong atom | Alloying |

### Line Defects (Dislocations)

- **Edge dislocation**: Extra half-plane of atoms
- **Screw dislocation**: Helical distortion

Dislocations allow plastic deformation.

### Planar Defects

- **Grain boundaries**: Between crystal regions
- **Stacking faults**: ABCABABC instead of ABCABC
- **Twin boundaries**: Mirror-image regions

## Miller Indices

Notation for crystal planes and directions.

### Planes
$$(hkl)$$

Example: (100) is perpendicular to x-axis.

### Directions
$$[uvw]$$

Example: [111] is body diagonal.

## X-Ray Diffraction

How we determine crystal structures.

### Bragg's Law
$$
n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta
$$

X-rays reflect off crystal planes. Constructive interference reveals plane spacing.

## Experiments

### Crystal Builder
Stack atoms in different arrangements. See Bravais lattices form.

### Defect Simulator
Introduce vacancies, interstitials. Watch how properties change.

### Diffraction Pattern
Shine X-rays on crystal. See diffraction spots. Deduce structure.

## Concepts

- **bravais-lattice**: 14 fundamental 3D lattice types
- **coordination-number**: Number of nearest neighbors
- **packing-efficiency**: Fraction of space filled
- **crystal-defect**: Imperfection in lattice

## Transition

Crystals provide structure. Now we explore how electrons move through materials: metals, insulators, and everything between.
